# Get Prediction Intervals

A confidence interval answers: where is the true mean? A prediction interval answers: where will
the next observed value fall? The prediction interval is always wider because it must account for
both uncertainty in the estimated mean and the irreducible noise in each individual observation
(the residual variance, σ²). Unlike confidence intervals, prediction intervals cannot shrink to
zero with more data (the observation-level noise remains no matter how large the sample).

## Fit

Fit a GAM on the motorcycle helmet dataset.

::: {#cfb84878 .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import whittaker as wk
import numpy as np

data = wk.load_dataset("mcycle")
model = wk.GAM("accel ~ s(times)").fit(data)
model.summary()
```

## Build a prediction grid

A 200-point grid spanning the full range of `times` is sufficient to compare both interval types.

::: {#4ea4dac3 .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
grid = {"times": np.linspace(data["times"].min(), data["times"].max(), 200)}
```
:::


## Confidence interval

Pass `interval="confidence"` to quantify uncertainty about the mean curve.

::: {#3fb63da4 .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
ci = model.predict(grid, interval="confidence")
ci_width = (ci.upper - ci.lower).mean().round(3)
ci_width
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3}
```
np.float64(23.081)
```
:::
:::


This width shrinks as sample size increases (it measures how well the mean is estimated).

## Prediction interval

Pass `interval="prediction"` to quantify where individual future observations are expected to
land.

::: {#e2c39a60 .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
pi = model.predict(grid, interval="prediction")
pi_width = (pi.upper - pi.lower).mean().round(3)
pi_width
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4}
```
np.float64(87.111)
```
:::
:::


The prediction interval is noticeably wider than the confidence interval. The excess comes from
the estimated residual variance, which is a property of the data-generating process and does not
decrease with sample size.

## Width ratio

Quantify how much wider the prediction interval is.

::: {#09a3a358 .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
round(pi_width / ci_width, 3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5}
```
np.float64(3.774)
```
:::
:::


A ratio well above 1 confirms that observation-level noise dominates the uncertainty. If the
model were fit on thousands of observations the confidence interval would nearly collapse, but the
prediction interval would remain wide by roughly the same absolute amount.

## Compare bounds directly

Inspect the first five rows of each set of bounds to see the difference concretely.

::: {#703c5b08 .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np

np.column_stack([
    ci.lower[:5].round(2),
    ci.upper[:5].round(2),
    pi.lower[:5].round(2),
    pi.upper[:5].round(2),
])
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6}
```
array([[-16.63,  23.16, -43.13,  49.67],
       [-14.66,  22.98, -41.79,  50.11],
       [-12.75,  22.85, -40.49,  50.59],
       [-10.92,  22.77, -39.25,  51.1 ],
       [ -9.18,  22.75, -38.07,  51.64]])
```
:::
:::


Columns are: CI lower, CI upper, PI lower, PI upper. The prediction bounds extend substantially
further from the fitted values.

## When to use each

Use `interval="confidence"` when you want to make statements about the mean response: "the
average acceleration at time 20 ms is between X and Y." Use `interval="prediction"` when you
need to bound where a new individual measurement will fall: "the next helmet test at 20 ms should
record a value between X and Y." Reporting prediction intervals as if they were confidence
intervals understates the true uncertainty for individual forecasts.
